Both REQ1 and REQ2
Neither REQ1 nor REQ2
questions.explanation: Need: P0 (8, 4, 2), P1 (3, 0, 0), P2 (1, 2, 2). Granting REQ1 leaves Available = (3, 2, 0): P1 can finish (Work (6, 4, 0)), but then P0 needs (8, 4, 0) and P2 needs (1, 2, 2), neither fits, and the state is unsafe. Granting REQ2 leaves Available = (1, 2, 2) and P1's Need (1, 0, 0): P1 finishes (Work (6, 4, 2)), then P2 (Work (8, 5, 3)), then P0 with Need (8, 4, 2). The state is safe, so only REQ2 is granted.

questions.stem: Two processes share Boolean variables S1 and S2, initialised to arbitrary values. Whenever P1 wants its critical section, it busy-waits while S1 == S2, runs the critical section, then executes S1 = S2. Whenever P2 wants its critical section, it busy-waits while S1 != S2, runs the critical section, then executes S2 = !S1. Between attempts, either process may stay in its remainder section for any length of time. Which statement is true?
options: Mutual exclusion is guaranteed, but progress is not.
Progress is guaranteed, but mutual exclusion is not.
Neither mutual exclusion nor progress is guaranteed.
Both mutual exclusion and progress are guaranteed.
questions.explanation: P1 may enter only when S1 ≠ S2 and P2 only when S1 = S2, and neither variable changes while a process is inside, so both can never be inside together. Each exit hands the turn to the other process (P1 makes S1 = S2, P2 makes S1 ≠ S2), so the processes must strictly alternate. If P1 stays in its remainder section, P2 can enter at most once more and is then locked out of a free section, which violates progress.

questions.stem: In Peterson's algorithm, P0 and P1 both want to enter, and each has already set its flag to true. P0 executes turn = 1, and only after that does P1 execute turn = 0. Neither has tested its while condition yet. What happens next?
options: P0 enters the critical section; P1 waits until P0 resets its flag.
P1 enters the critical section; P0 waits until P1 resets its flag.
Both wait forever, because each sees the other's flag set.
Both may enter, because each of them wrote turn.
questions.explanation: The final value of turn is 0, written last by P1. P0 waits only while flag[1] && turn == 1, which is false, so P0 enters. P1 waits while flag[0] && turn == 0, which is true, so it spins until P0 leaves and sets flag[0] = false. The process that writes turn last defers to the other.

questions.stem: Processes guard a critical section with a spinlock: the entry code is while (TestAndSet(&lock)); and the exit code is lock = false, where TestAndSet is atomic and lock starts false. Which requirement of a critical-section solution can this lock fail to meet?
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
None; it meets all three
questions.explanation: Only one TestAndSet can see false and take the lock, so mutual exclusion holds, and when the lock is free some spinning process succeeds, so progress holds. Nothing decides who wins after a release, though: a process can release the lock and take it again before a particular waiter tests it, any number of times, so that waiter's wait has no bound.

questions.stem: A producer and a consumer share an unbounded buffer, with semaphores n = 0 (items in the buffer) and s = 1 (buffer lock). The producer loops: produce; wait(s); add item; signal(s); signal(n). The consumer loops: wait(s); wait(n); remove item; signal(s); consume. Which statement is true?
options: The code is correct: the consumer never removes from an empty buffer and nothing deadlocks.
The consumer may remove an item from an empty buffer.
Deadlock is possible: the consumer can block on n while holding s, so the producer can never add an item.
The producer may block forever in wait(n).
questions.explanation: If the consumer runs when the buffer is empty, it takes s and then blocks in wait(n) while still holding s. The producer then blocks in wait(s) and can never add the item that would release the consumer, so both are stuck. The consumer cannot remove from an empty buffer because wait(n) guards removal, and the producer never waits on n. Swapping the consumer's two waits fixes the code.

questions.stem: In the first readers-writers solution, readers share read_count, protected by mutex, and writers use the semaphore rw_mutex. What does a reader do when its increment makes read_count equal to 1?
options: It performs wait(rw_mutex), locking writers out on behalf of all readers.
It performs signal(rw_mutex), letting a waiting writer start.
It performs wait(mutex) a second time to keep other readers out.
Nothing extra; only writers ever touch rw_mutex.
questions.explanation: The first reader to arrive must make sure no writer is active and keep writers out while any reader remains, so it waits on rw_mutex. Later readers only increment read_count and go in. The last reader to leave, the one that brings read_count back to 0, performs signal(rw_mutex).

questions.stem: Which statement about monitors with condition variables is correct?
options: A signal(c) on a condition with no waiting process is remembered and wakes the next process that calls wait(c).
Under Mesa semantics, a woken process must re-test its condition in a while loop before going on.
Two processes may run monitor procedures at once if they wait on different condition variables.
Under Hoare semantics, the signalling process keeps running and the woken process waits for the monitor to become free.
questions.explanation: Under Mesa semantics the signaller keeps the monitor and the woken process runs only later, by which time another process may have changed the state, so it must re-check its condition in a loop. A signal with no waiter is lost, a monitor admits one active process whatever the conditions, and under Hoare semantics it is the signaller that suspends.

questions.stem: Five philosophers share five chopsticks, one between each neighbouring pair, and each needs both adjacent chopsticks to eat. Which of these rules guarantee that deadlock cannot occur?
options: At most four philosophers may sit at the table at any time.
Every philosopher picks up the left chopstick first, then the right one.
Chopsticks are numbered 0–4 and every philosopher picks up the lower-numbered of the two first.
Philosopher 0 picks up the right chopstick first; all the others pick up the left one first.
questions.explanation: With four philosophers seated and five chopsticks, at least one of them can get both. Taking the lower-numbered chopstick first is a global resource order, so no circular wait can form, and one philosopher taking the right chopstick first breaks the cycle in the same way. Left then right for everyone lets all five hold their left chopstick and wait forever for the right.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about resource-allocation graphs and deadlock are true?
options: If every resource type has a single instance, a cycle in the graph means the processes on it are deadlocked.
If resource types have several instances, a cycle in the graph means the processes on it are deadlocked.
If the graph has no cycle, no process is deadlocked.
A system in an unsafe state is already deadlocked.
questions.explanation: With single instances a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. With several instances a process outside the cycle may release an instance and break it, so a cycle is necessary but not sufficient. No cycle means no circular wait, hence no deadlock. An unsafe state only means deadlock can no longer be ruled out; the processes may still all finish.

questions.stem: Binary semaphores a, b, c and d all start at 1. Processes X, Y and Z each perform wait() on three of them in the order shown, run a critical section, then signal all three. Which choice of orders can never deadlock?
options: X: a, b, c; Y: b, c, d; Z: c, d, a
X: b, a, c; Y: b, c, d; Z: a, c, d
X: b, a, c; Y: c, b, d; Z: a, c, d
X: a, b, c; Y: c, b, d; Z: c, d, a
questions.explanation: With X: b, a, c, Y: b, c, d and Z: a, c, d, every process waits in an order consistent with the single ranking b < a < c < d, so no cycle of waits can form. Each other choice has a cycle. In the first, X holds a and waits for b, Y holds b and waits for c, and Z holds c and d and waits for a. In the third, X holds b and waits for a, Z holds a and waits for c, and Y holds c and waits for b. In the fourth, X holds a and b and waits for c while Y holds c and waits for b.

questions.stem: A system numbers its resource types and requires every process to request resources only in increasing order of their numbers. Which necessary condition for deadlock does this rule deny?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
questions.explanation: A process holding resource i can wait only for a resource numbered above i, so any chain of waits climbs strictly in number and can never close into a cycle. Processes still hold resources exclusively, still hold while waiting, and still cannot be preempted; only circular wait is ruled out.

pitfalls.text: The four Coffman conditions are necessary, not sufficient: with multi-instance resources a cycle can exist without a deadlock.
In producer-consumer, wait(full) or wait(empty) must come before wait(mutex); reversing them can put a process to sleep while it holds the buffer lock.
An unsafe state is not a deadlock: it only means the system can no longer guarantee that every process will finish.
Detection compares each process's current Request with Work; Banker's avoidance compares Need = Max − Allocation. Swapping them gives wrong answers.
The Banker's algorithm must be run on every request before it is granted, not once at start-up.
A counting semaphore initialised to k > 1 lets k processes into a section together, so updates to shared data can still be lost.
Peterson's algorithm is a two-process solution, and on modern hardware it needs memory fences to stay correct.
A monitor's signal(c) with no waiting process is lost, whereas a counting semaphore's signal is remembered in its count; a binary semaphore already at 1 loses it too.

S = 1 for mutual exclusion, S = 0 for ordering

Prevent: break one condition; ordered requests break circular wait

errata.claim: Deadlock detection uses the wait-for graph, and a cycle means deadlock.
errata.correction: A wait-for graph works only when every resource type has a single instance. With multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient, so detection must run the matrix algorithm on Available, Allocation and the current Request of each process.

errata.claim: With multiple instances, detection runs the safety algorithm, and the deadlocked processes are those left with Finish = false.
errata.correction: Detection compares each process's current Request, not its Need (Max − Allocation), with Work, and processes that hold no resources start with Finish = true. Run on Need, the loop only tests safety, and an unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock.
